summary.value: The paper maps natural-language advice into a formal DSL (RLang) that can express multiple MDP components, plans/policies, rewards, and transition effects, and plugs those components into a Dyna-Q–style planner (RLang-Dyna-Q). A two-stage LLM pipeline “grounds” free-form text into executable RLang. A lightweight VLM step helps disambiguate object references. On MiniGrid and VirtualHome tasks, injecting RLang advice improves sample efficiency and final performance versus vanilla Dyna-Q, with ablations showing different gains from plan/policy/effect advice. A small user study suggests non-experts can produce useful advice when guided by the DSL.

strengths.value: A clear, unified way to use language beyond rewards or policies alone, covering multiple MDP elements. Simple integration with model-based planning (Dyna-Q) that yields consistent empirical gains. Interpretable advice that can be inspected, edited, and ablated. Practical grounding pipeline (LLM + optional VLM) that reduces manual engineering, and clean experiments that isolate the contribution of plan/policy/effect advice, highlighting when language helps most.

weaknesses.value:
Q1: The method is built around Dyna-Q/Q-learning. There are no head-to-head comparisons against strong, commonly used algorithms (e.g., PPO, SAC, TD3/A2C). Without modern baselines, external validity is limited.

Q2: While plan/policy/effect are separated, the paper lacks a principled study of when each type helps (task difficulty, horizon, sparsity) and how types interact. There’s no prescriptive guidance for choosing or composing advice across tasks.

Q3: Language grounding relies on fixed in-context prompting. There is no trainable module (fine-tuning, preference optimization, RLHF, self-correction) and no comparison showing when learning-based alignment would outperform ICL.

Q4: The contribution largely extends prior RLang by plugging language-derived components into Dyna-Q planning. The algorithmic novelty feels incremental.

Q5: The paper lacks controlled curves of environment steps vs. performance with matched compute. Model-call counts, planning steps, and replay budgets are not normalized, risking unfair comparisons.

Q6: Evaluations focus on discrete/grid or constrained household tasks. There are no results for continuous control, high-dimensional vision with long horizons/sparse rewards, or cross-task transfer (zero/low-shot).

Q7: Results emphasize success/return but lack analyses of variance/stability (seed sensitivity), exploration efficiency, convergence speed, policy complexity, interpretability, and quantitative “advice dependence” (usage rates, ablations).

comment.value:
We thank the reviewer for their feedback on our work, and especially thank them for acknowledging the central contribution of this paper: the notion that language should ground to every component of the MDP.

We appreciate the concerns raised by the reviewer, and have decided to add an additional paragraph just before the discussion section of the paper to address weaknesses 2 and 3:

> Beyond the grounding of object symbols, we note that our translation method assumes access to robust semantics for notions of action (e.g., \texttt{go\_to}) and perception (e.g., \texttt{is\_at}). Without the relevant conceptual groundings for notions in language advice, translation into a formal specification language would be purposeless. To ameliorate the need for concept semantics, we chose a set of environments with a reduced state space that was easy to define semantics over. We leave the discovery and learning of concept semantics to future work.
> 

In short, we agree with both claims, that choosing low-dimensional MDPs and hand-specifying semantics in RLang are limiting factors. However, we note again that the central contribution of the work is the claim that language ought to be grounded to every component of the MDP, and ergo our goal was to demonstrate that as best as possible in minimal and interpretable examples. We acknowledge the need for future work to address these limitations, but do not believe they detract from the overall ideological stance the paper aims to make.

Regarding the reviewer’s questions about the translation pipeline, it is a fixed two-stage LLM translation pipeline that leverages few-shot translation with in-context examples (between 3 and 5 static examples for each translation). API calls to GPT4 were used to perform the translation, and we argue that the ability to leverage an off-the-shelf LLM without any fine-tuning is a point of strength for our theoretical claim because it indicates that RLang provides a sufficiently expressive semantic representation that requires minimal learning to translate language to. We included additional prompt details in the appendix, and are happy to include any information the reviewer finds relevant.

We note that our pipeline does not override advice whatsoever. Our goal is to provide a direct translation of language advice, improvements to agent performance are an indication that the advice was useful, and our pipeline will faithfully represent poor or contradictory advice (see Figure 5 for an example). The reviewer rightfully raises questions about ambiguity of language translation, however our approach assumes clear and unambiguous advice given in good faith for instructing a human to perform a task.

We kindly ask the reviewer to consider revising their rating, and to consider whether the ideological claims made in this paper would be of value to the ICLR community.

summary.value: Reviewers concern mainly on experiment evaluations. Authors' rebuttal addressed part of them, but there are still some major concerns unsolved (see below). Hence I recommend for rejection.

reviewer_concerns.value:
Addressed concerns:  (1) The authors clarified that symbols (like $\epsilon$, $\gamma$) follow standard RL literature and committed to expanding the background section, which directly addressed Reviewer ouWK's confusion. (2) The authors clarified that Q-table updates are controlled across experiments (matching Dyna-Q updates to RLang-Dyna-Q updates), addressing Reviewer pEzx's concern about unfair comparisons. (3) The concern regarding the high cost of manual annotation (Reviewer BVMZ) was mitigated by the authors' demonstration of using Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to automate the generation of vocabulary files, though the robustness of this remains a minor open question.


Outstanding Concerns: 

(1). Multiple reviewers (pEzx, BVMZ) criticized the use of Dyna-Q as the sole baseline and the lack of comparison to modern algorithms (PPO, SAC). The authors did not add new baselines.

(2). The restriction to simple, discrete grid-worlds (MiniGrid, VirtualHome) remains a significant limitation. The authors acknowledged this but dismissed it as "future work," leaving the method's viability in continuous or complex domains unproven.

(3). Reviewer pEzx’s concern that the method relies on static, few-shot LLM prompting (rather than a trainable/learnable module) was defended by the authors as a "strength" (ease of use), but the technical concern regarding the system's inability to learn or self-correct remains valid.

(4). Concerns about safety, hallucination, and handling conflicting advice (Reviewer ouWK) were acknowledged with a promise to add a limitations paragraph, but no mechanism was introduced to actually solve these issues in the proposed algorithm.

reviewer_scores.value: I think reviewers will maintain their scores as most concerns are not fully addressed.

summary.value: The paper proposes a method to ground natural language advices into RLang, a formal language for specifying Markov Decision Processes (MDPs). The main hypothesis is that pieces of advice can map to different components of the MDP such as policies, reward functions, transition functions, and plans whereas most existing methods map all advice to a single element. The authors introduce a two-step LLM-based pipeline that (i) classifies each piece of advice according to its most suitable MDP component and (ii) translates it into an executable RLang program. They further present RLang-Dyna-Q, a modified version of Dyna-Q capable of integrating RLang-derived specifications. Experiments are conducted on several environments, and ablations are provided to test the main hypothesis.

strengths.value:
- The central hypothesis that different forms of natural language advices naturally correspond to different MDP components is conceptually sound and practically relevant.
- The proposed framework provides a novel perspective on how symbolic formal languages like RLang can be integrated with LLMs to inform reinforcement learning.

weaknesses.value:
- The background section reads more as a related works section than as a formal introduction to notation and core concepts. While RLang is introduced, its explanation is insufficient for readers unfamiliar with it to fully grasp how RLang programs are structured or what components such as “vocabularies” represent.    
- The main algorithm is not clearly presented. The pseudocode omits explanations for several hyperparameters and integration mechanisms. For example, many symbols (e.g., $N_1, N_2$) are undefined, and their purpose or selection criteria are not discussed.
- The technical contribution appears modest. Much of the implementation relies on prompting large language models for translation, with limited algorithmic innovation beyond that.
- Limitations are not discussed properly. Translation via LLMs introduces hallucination and instability. The only mitigation provided consists in restricting vocabulary through prompting, while is helpful it is insufficient to ensure reliable grounding.
- Experiments are limited to small, discrete environments and are sometimes under-explained. There is no evaluation of translation accuracy, only indirect validation through task performance. Also, the central hypothesis is verified only in two experiments (MidMazeLava, FoodSafety) in the other two ablation is missing (HardMaze) or other baselines surpass it (CouchPotato).
- The method still depends heavily on hand-specified vocabularies, which raises questions about automation and scalability, even though the authors later explore partial automation using vision-language models.

questions.value:
- Can you comment on how to extend this approach beyond tabular settings to continuous or real-world domains?
- How do you ensure safety in a real-world deployement of this method, especially when LLM generated translations may hallucinate?
- How does the system handle inconsistent or conflicting pieces of advice?
- Why in HardMaze there is no ablation with other variants?

The paper presents a promising direction by connecting natural language grounding with the internal structure of MDPs. However, the current implementation and evaluation feels immature. The approach heavily relies on prompting, and several methodological details are missing. Suggested improvements are: a clearer presentation of the algorithm, a comprehensive discussion of limitations, and stronger experimental validation for instance considerin translation accuracy and extension beyond tabular.

summary.value: The work proposes a method to provide natural language advice to RL agents by mapping to RLang as an intermediary step. The work also ensures that the the mapping to RLang incorporates all elements of an MDP, differing from prior work which typically incorporate advice for portion of the MDP, like the transition dynamics. The paper the presents two important steps from this, 1) by showing a clear method to incorporate this RLang advice into Dyna-Q which demonstrates its utility, 2) showing that vision-language models can be used to structure the RLang vocabulary files to avoid needing human supervision.

strengths.value:
## Originality
The work is fairly original - it is clearly grounded in the prior work on RLang and the literature on incorporating feedback into pieces of the MDP. However, this is clearly mentioned and ultimately this clarity supports the originality of the work. At the very least I do not believe it should be help against this work. The final experiments connecting vision-language models also supports the originality as it takes on slight step further and incorporates other ideas like foundation models.

## Quality
The hypothesis of the work and the problem it aims to solve is clearly stated. Experiments are designed well to directly evaluate the core claims of the work and the results are evaluated fairly.

## Clarity
Overall the paper is well written, figures are clear and the examples used are chosen well to demonstrate the utility of the proposed method. The paper is also well structured to be a natural read and gradually introduces new idea or addresses lingering concerns (like the need for supervision). I appreciate the effort and clarity of Algorithm 1.

## Significance
The work addresses a core and widely applicable problem - how to incorporate guiding language into the RL pipeline. This has implications for research in safety and other key areas of concern beyond just academia.

weaknesses.value:
## Quality
I have two primary concerns for quality: 1) the experiments shown in Figures 2, 3 and 4 only compare to Dyna-Q. While this is certainly an obvious baseline but means that the experimental design of the work is ablation which does not compare to different ideas or approaches. It is predictable that the model with the most information will perform the best in this ablation. Especially since the paper does go to great lengths to justify the approach relative to other works, it would have been appropriate to compare to these other works. 2) the need for supervision is acknowledge but it is a bit ask. Additionally, and my bigger concern, the section that aims to counter the need for supervision suggests that a foundation vision-language model is needed. This is not given sufficient consideration as the need for a foundation model to assist with data labelling brings in many important concerns (such as reliability and training costs) which are ignored. While I appreciate the authors aiming to remove the need for human labelling, it is still necessary to fully discuss the implications for using a foundation model as this is at best a partial solution.

## Clarity
Two fairly minor things: 1) the bottom of page 3 has a sentence which stop half-way through. The caption of Figure 6 is not rendered properly.

## Significance
Footnote 1 bothers me slightly as this does not seem trivial to solve and is (to my intuitive understanding) the biggest problem with trying to incorporate natural language into all pieces of an MDP: there is ambiguity in this process and it becomes more difficult to extract the key pieces and represent more text in terms of RLang. So this does limit the significance of the work to me, since how to extend to a case where each piece of advice grounds to multiple types, is not explored.

questions.value:
How would subsequent work go about addressing the limitation of Footnote 1?

How robust is the proposed model against noise or errors from the vision-language model labelling?

How does the RLang Dyna-Q compare to SOTA models for the domains in Figures 2 to 4?

comment.value:
We appreciate the reviewer for their detailed comments, and we believe that the weaknesses they raise can be ameliorated by a discussion on the purpose of the work. Some of the weaknesses raised are more fitting for works that claim to provide a “be all, end all” solution to language grounding, or for works that present SOTA RL algorithms, or works that provide practical tips for language grounding. Our goal is **not** to provide a ready-made, off-the-shelf, solution for language grounding with practical tips and guidance, but **to advance the theoretical claim** that language ought to be grounded to every component of an MDP, and how one might do that by using a formal specification language (RLang).

The unique contribution of this work is precisely the notion that language should ground to all components of the MDP, and the experiments, demonstrations, and user study we ran all serve this ideological claim. The ablation studies also supplement the evidence for the idea that various kinds of language advice have natural groundings in various parts of the MDP, which can be integrated into a learning agent. Our choice of DynaQ as a baseline agent was motivated by the need to integrate various components of the decision-process into a single agent (e.g., goals and plans and transitions and rewards). The most harmonious way to achieve this is via a model-based RL agent, and since our goal is not to provide a SOTA solution but to advance the theoretical claim that language should ground to every component of the MDP, DynaQ is a sufficient choice as a base RL agent.

The difficulty of grounding language to continuous control environments should not be understated. Again, this work serves to plant the flag that language should ground to all components of an MDP, and we believe future work can address the grounding of language to continuous control, high-dimensional state spaces, etc. **Our bottom line is that this ideological statement is valuable to the community**, which we have already seen build upon the central claims made in the work. We hope the community continues to build on this central claim, which we believe is well-substantiated and stands on its own well enough. We kindly ask the reviewer to consider revising their rating, and we implore them for additional feedback and commentary.

We also note that the Q-table updates are controlled for in all experiments, i.e. DynaQ makes the same number of Q updates per iteration that RLang-DynaQ does.

Thank you.

I thank the authors for their response. While I appreciate the "ideological" contribution of grounding language to all MDP components, and acknowledge the effort in building the translation pipeline, I find the current work to be more of a preliminary proof-of-concept rather than a rigorous technical contribution expected for ICLR.

My main concerns remain:

Theoretical Rigor: The paper proposes a framework but lacks deep theoretical derivations to support its properties.

Empirical Strength: The validation relies on Dyna-Q in simple environments without comparisons to modern, strong baselines.

While the core idea is innovative and goes beyond pure conjecture, the execution and validation feel somewhat thin for the main track. Therefore, I will maintain my score.

We thank the reviewer for their thorough comments, and especially thank them for their generous explanation of the strengths of our paper. We’ve tried to address their concerns below.

We first want to address the quality and significance weaknesses raised by the reviewer, primarily the choice of DynaQ as a base agent, the need for semantic supervision — later addressed by a VLM, and the limiting assumption we made regarding individual grounding targets for language advice.

Our choice of DynaQ as a baseline agent was motivated by the need to integrate various components of the decision-process into a single agent (e.g., goals and plans and transitions and rewards). The most harmonious way to achieve this is via a model-based RL agent, and since our goal is not to provide a SOTA solution but to advance the theoretical claim that language should ground to every component of the MDP, DynaQ is a sufficient choice as a base RL agent. Yes, it is intuitive that the agent with more information will perform the best, but the implementation of a pipeline and agent that can ***effectively utilize*** this information is non-trivial, and a central part of the contribution of the work.

Regarding the semantic supervision of specifying conceptual structure to ground language to, which is later partially addressed with a VLM, we raise that difficulty of grounding language the world cannot be understated, and we do not claim to provide a complete and total solution to the language grounding problem. Absolutely, the work provides a partial solution to this extremely difficult open problem in the field. Specifically, our work advances the theoretical claim that **the approaches we take for language grounding** should ground to every component of the MDP in order to be considered complete. We are happy to address this more clearly in the work directly if that helps.

We agree that the assumption made about the singular grounding of language advice is limiting, however we argue that the primary thesis of the work is again that language should ground to every component of the MDP. Therefore, while the assumption is limiting for our specific implementation, it does not harm the theoretical claims that our work substantiates. There are many ways this limitation could be addressed in future work, by e.g. attempting to ground multiple translations, engineering a richer translation pipeline, etc.

We kindly ask the reviewer to consider revising their rating, keeping in mind that the work was written to contribute the idea that language should ground to every component of an MDP, and that the experiments, demonstrations, and user studies run in the paper work well to serve this goal.

We will adjust any formatting issues in the final submission.

• Why in HardMaze there is no ablation with other variants?

The purpose of this experiment is to demonstrate that an RLang agent with complete facility of language can perform well in a task in which the baseline agent **can not accrue any reward** **whatsoever**. In all the other experiments, the baseline agent is capable of accruing reward. We will re-order the experiments so the ablations are together, to clear up confusion.

We appreciate the reviewers criticisms on discussion of limitations. We have included the following paragraph just before the discussion section:

> Beyond the grounding of object symbols, we note that our translation method assumes access to robust semantics for notions of action (e.g., \texttt{go\_to}) and perception (e.g., \texttt{is\_at}). Without the relevant conceptual groundings for the words in language advice, translation into a formal specification language would be purposeless. To ameliorate the need for concept semantics, we chose a set of environments with a relatively small and interpretable state space that was easy to define semantics over. We leave the discovery and learning of concept semantics to future work.
> 

We also acknowledge the limitations of LLMs as poor translators/hallucinators, however we argue that advancements in LLMs could address these issues. We note that while we used LLMs in our pipeline, the main contribution is the notion that language should ground to every component of the MDP, and that other methods of semantic parsing could obviate the need for LLMs entirely.

What else should we include in the above paragraph to adequately discuss the limitations of this work?

We again thank the reviewer for their criticisms. We hope that we have addressed their concerns well enough for them to reconsider their score, and are happy to take any additional questions and feedback.

summary.value: This paper presents RLang-Dyna-Q, a novel model-based reinforcement learning framework designed to leverage natural language advice. The core contribution is a system that translates human language into a formal, grounded language (RLang) capable of specifying information about all core components of an MDP—policies, rewards, transition functions, and plans. By integrating this structured advice into a Dyna-Q-style algorithm, the agent's learning is significantly accelerated. The authors validate their approach with strong empirical results and further demonstrate a promising method for automating the symbol-grounding process using Vision-Language Models (VLMs), reducing reliance on manual annotation.

strengths.value:
1. The core concept of grounding language to all MDP elements is original.
2. The experiments clearly show significant gains in sample efficiency and final performance, validating the framework's effectiveness.

weaknesses.value:
1.  The paper could benefit from more details on the natural language to RLang translator. Its robustness to varied or ambiguous phrasing is critical, and more information on its architecture, training needs, and failure modes would strengthen the work.
2. The experiments are conducted in environments with relatively low-dimensional state spaces. A more thorough discussion or experimentation on scaling the grounding approach to high-dimensional inputs (e.g., raw pixels) would be valuable.
3. While powerful, the RLang formalism might impose a significant cognitive load on human users. The practicality of authoring complex advice by hand could be a limitation and warrants discussion.

questions.value:
1.  Could you elaborate on the architecture of the natural language-to-RLang translator? What are its data requirements for effective training?
2.  How does the framework handle incorrect or conflicting advice? Can the agent learn to override flawed advice based on its own environmental experience?

comment.value:
We thank the reviewer for the criticisms, which we address below.

In regards to the DynaQ algorithm, we are more than happy to elaborate on the symbols used, though many of them are commonplace in the RL literature (e.g. epsilon, gamma). Aside from N_1 and N_2, which represent the number of Q updates from the environment model and the RLang model, respectively. Which other hyperparameters do you believe need clarification? We use the same symbols used in the description of the original DynaQ algorithm. Clear information about DynaQ parameters can easily be gathered with background reading.

Regarding the criticism of the background section, we argue that it is reasonable to expect readers of this work to consult the paper that presents RLang, especially considering the complexity of the RLang language. We chose to discuss RLang at a level of abstraction that would serve the claims in the paper, and that was primarily at a high-level as being a language about various MDP components. We wanted to be forthcoming with the vocabulary files we used, which represent additional environment-specific semantics for the language (similar to defining classes and variables in Python). An example RLang vocabulary that was used in the virtualhome experiments can be seen in the Appendix (section A.2), we hope this clears up any confusion.

We push back against the idea that our technical contribution is minimal. To elaborate, our technical contribution is the combination of a two-stage pipeline for language translation of natural language into RLang (described in Sec 3 with exact prompt examples for both stages in the Appendix, see e.g. A.3), as well as an RLang-enabled DynaQ agent that is capable of leveraging information about partial plans, policies, transition functions, and reward functions (see Sec 3.1). To the best of our knowledge, no other work has supplied an agent that can faithfully integrate every single component of the MDP into learning.

• Can you comment on how to extend this approach beyond tabular settings to continuous or real-world domains?

Applying this approach beyond the tabular setting would rely on 1) algorithmic advances in the agent, e.g. by migrating to a deep model-based agent that can process continuous observations and produce continuous actions; and 2) advances in the formation of concept semantics from continuous representations, e.g. prescribing or learning such notions as “cat” or “go_to” from direct continuous percepts and actions.  We note again that the central contribution of the work is the claim that language ought to be grounded to every component of the MDP, and ergo our goal was to demonstrate that as best as possible in minimal and interpretable examples. We believe that future works that incorporate continuous actions and percepts can be done in the same spirit as this work: they can ground language to all components of the MDP.

• How do you ensure safety in a real-world deployement of this method, especially when LLM generated translations may hallucinate?

Our goal is not to provide a ready-made, off-the-shelf, solution for language grounding with practical tips and guidance, but to advance the theoretical claim that language ought to be grounded to every component of an MDP, and how one might do that by using a formal specification language (RLang). We acknowledge the need for safety constraints for any real-world deployment of this method, but our implementation is chiefly designed to advance theoretical claims and we leave questions about deployment to the broader research community.

• How does the system handle inconsistent or conflicting pieces of advice?

Our goal is to provide a direct translation of language advice. Improvements to agent performance are only an indication that the advice was useful. Our pipeline will faithfully represent poor or contradictory advice (see Figure 5 for an example, as you pointed out).
